Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

BUILD: one real proof-of-concept foundation for "Kodely Pro" — the tier that generates full applications rather than marketing sites.

## Read the plan first
The board is SQLite at `C:\Users\edmem\OneDrive\Desktop\Kodely\Kodely Board\board.sqlite` (`node:sqlite`, `DatabaseSync`, **READ ONLY — never write to it**). Board id `720aa8c1-d259-4e49-b777-c58965efabd1`, column `Kodely Pro — Full Apps`, 41 cards. **Read the DECISION cards first** — the research concluded that the blocker is architectural, not a prompting problem, and those cards carry the options and a recommendation.

## The thesis you are testing
The owner's idea is that pre-built foundations for app types (CRM, booking, inventory) make generation both **easier and credit-cheaper**, because the model writes less. **That is a measurable claim and this task is the measurement.**

## The constraint that decides the shape
Read `lib/foundation.ts`, `lib/build-site.ts`, `app/api/site/[slug]/**` (the CSP), and `lib/agent.ts`. Generated sites are static, `react` + `react-dom` only, no npm install per generation, `connect-src 'none'` — **no server, no database, no auth, no network.**

So a shared, multi-user CRM is not reachable. A **single-user, client-only** app absolutely is: `localStorage` or IndexedDB gives real persistence on one device with no backend at all. That is a genuine product for a sole trader tracking clients or bookings, and it is honest about what it is.

**Build the client-only version.** Do not pretend it is multi-user, and make the foundation itself say so.

## Deliver
1. **`lib/foundations/` — one complete, working app foundation.** Pick the strongest candidate from the board (a simple CRM/client tracker or a booking/appointment log) and build it properly: data model, persistence layer, list/detail/create/edit, empty states, and the same quality bar `lib/agent.ts` demands of generated sites (responsive to 380px, dark mode, real focus states, no external requests).
2. **Prove it compiles** through `buildSite` from `lib/build-site.ts`. Load `.env` first — `KODELY_FOUNDATION_DIR` must be set or the path falls back to a Linux default and every build fails with a misleading "Cannot find module".
3. **MEASURE THE CREDIT CLAIM.** Count the tokens in the foundation versus what the model would have to write without it. You do not need to run a real generation to do this usefully — compare file sizes and reason about what `describeFiles()` re-sends per turn versus what the model would otherwise author. **Show the arithmetic.** If the foundation turns out to make builds *more* expensive (it is re-sent on every turn as context), say so plainly — that would be the most valuable finding here and it is a real possibility.
4. **A short `docs/pro-foundations.md`**: what this foundation is, what it honestly cannot do, and what the next 3-4 would be.

## Scope — ONLY: `lib/foundations/**` and `docs/pro-foundations.md`
DO NOT modify: lib/foundation.ts, lib/agent.ts, lib/build-site.ts, prisma/schema.prisma, any other lib file, app/**, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json. If wiring it in needs a change elsewhere, describe it precisely in your report.

## Constraints
- **No new npm dependencies**, for the foundation or the repo. That is the architectural constraint, not a preference.
- Data lives on the device. Say so in the UI — a user must never believe their client list is backed up when it is one browser-cache clear from gone. That honesty is the whole difference between this being a product and being a trap.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npx eslint app lib components`, and `node --import ./scripts/test/register.mjs --test "tests/*.test.mjs"` must ALL pass — currently 0 errors, 0 warnings, 209 tests.**

## Report back
Which foundation you built and why that one, proof it compiles, **the credit arithmetic with your actual numbers and an honest verdict on whether the thesis holds**, what it cannot do, and what would have to change architecturally for a genuinely multi-user app.

########## [0] DECISION: pick the backend architecture for Pro apps
Nothing else in this plan can start until this is answered. A CRM needs data that outlives a browser tab, users who log in, and queries that run somewhere the user cannot tamper with. Today a generated site is static files in Postgres rows, served under `connect-src 'none'` — it cannot make a single network request. Four real options:

(1) CLIENT-ONLY (IndexedDB/localStorage). Zero infrastructure change, works under today's CSP unchanged. Genuinely fine for a single-user tracker. Fatal for anything shared: no second device, no second user, no backup, and 'clear site data' destroys a business's customer list. Verdict: ship it (see the local-only apps card) but it is NOT the Pro tier.

(2) KODELY-HOSTED BaaS — one first-party multi-tenant data service at a single origin, with declarative per-project schemas, first-party end-user auth, and server-enforced row scoping. Requires exactly ONE new entry in connect-src. The agent writes ZERO backend code — it declares a schema and writes UI. Verdict: RECOMMENDED.

(3) PER-PROJECT DATABASE PROVISIONING (Neon/Supabase branch per project). Real isolation, real portability. But: nonzero cost from day one for projects that are mostly abandoned, a third-party provisioning call on the critical path of generation, and — decisively — the agent must then write schema, policies and queries, which is both the expensive part and the part where competitors have shipped real authorization holes. Verdict: reject for v1, keep as the 'eject' path.

(4) EMBEDDED SQLITE/PGlite IN THE BROWSER. Gives real SQL but not sharing — same fatal flaw as (1) — and PGlite ships ~3MB of .wasm, which `readDistTree` in lib/build-site.ts silently drops (TEXT_EXTENSIONS has no .wasm) and which trips the 2MB per-file cap anyway. Verdict: reject.

RECOMMENDATION: (2), with (1) shipped first as a cheap de-risking step and (3) offered later as an anti-lock-in escape hatch. Owner must confirm before any foundation work starts.

########## [1] DECISION: are we willing to open connect-src at all
`connect-src 'none'` in app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts is the single control that stops a generated site phoning home. docs/security/audit-2026-08.md leans on it explicitly: it is the reason finding H1 (sites served from the app's own origin at kodely.me/api/site/...) is rated High rather than Critical — script on a published page cannot call /api/* with the victim's cookies because fetch is dead.

Every backend option except client-only requires relaxing it. So this decision has a hard prerequisite the owner needs to accept up front: H1 must be fixed FIRST. If published sites still render on kodely.me when connect-src opens, we have hostile first-party script that can now also make network calls — that is a materially worse position than the audit describes today.

The relaxation itself can be narrow: `connect-src https://data.kodely.app` and deliberately NOT `'self'`, so a Pro app can reach the data service and nothing else, including our own app API. Combined with the audit's M4 fix (`form-action`, `base-uri`, `object-src`), which must land at the same time because a Pro app legitimately shows a login form and is therefore a far better phishing shell than a marketing page.

If the owner is not willing to move site serving to a separate registrable domain, Pro cannot ship with a network backend. That is the honest answer and it is a business decision, not an engineering one.

########## [2] DECISION: does Kodely become a processor for customers' end-user data
This is the biggest decision in the plan and it is not technical. Today Kodely holds its own users' data. The moment a plumber's CRM built on Kodely holds that plumber's customer list — names, phone numbers, addresses, job notes, possibly payment references — Kodely is processing personal data on behalf of a business customer.

What that actually obliges: a data processing agreement offered to every Pro customer; a documented sub-processor list; breach notification duties to the customer within a fixed window; the ability to honour a deletion or export request that arrives about a person Kodely has no relationship with; a retention policy per app, not just per Kodely account (lib/retention.ts covers Kodely's own tables only); and a defensible answer to 'where is the data' for customers outside the US.

The worst version of this is a booking app for a therapist or a client portal for a law firm, which pulls in health and legal-privilege data. Recommendation: proceed, but with an explicit acceptable-use line in the Pro terms that prohibits health, financial-account and government-ID data at launch, and revisit once there is a real compliance posture. The alternative — client-only apps forever — is a smaller business but carries none of this.

Blocked on the owner. Nothing about foundations should be built until there is an answer, because 'we will host your customers' data' is the actual product being sold.

########## [3] DECISION: one shared dependency tree, or one per foundation family
lib/build-site.ts symlinks every build's node_modules at one shared, pre-installed tree (KODELY_FOUNDATION_DIR, installed once by scripts/install-foundation.mjs). That tree currently ships exactly react and react-dom as runtime dependencies. App foundations will want more: a router, a schema/validation library, a date library for booking availability, probably a table and a chart.

Option A — grow the one tree. Simplest, but every free-tier marketing-site build then compiles against a much larger dependency graph it never uses, and every dependency added is code that runs inside `vite build` on our server, so the blast radius of a compromised package now includes every user.

Option B — a second tree (e.g. KODELY_FOUNDATION_DIR_APP) and a `foundation` parameter on buildSite(). Roughly a ten-line change in lib/build-site.ts plus a column on Project recording which foundation a project was created from. Keeps the marketing-site path byte-identical to what is running and audited today, and means a dependency added for the CRM cannot affect a plumber's landing page.

RECOMMENDATION: Option B. The isolation is nearly free and it means the Pro dependency set can move fast without re-risking the product that currently works.

########## [4] DECISION: Pro is a subscription, not a bigger credit pack
Credits are defined in lib/credits.ts as a fixed amount of MODEL SPEND — one credit is $0.002 of Anthropic tokens. That definition is the whole anti-bill-shock contract and it should not be quietly broadened.

But a Pro app introduces a cost class Kodely has never had: cost that recurs whether or not anyone generates anything. A live CRM holds rows, serves API requests, stores files and sends emails every month, forever, off a build that was paid for once. Selling that through credits alone means every successful Pro customer becomes progressively less profitable — the opposite of how it should work.

So Pro needs two components: a monthly subscription that covers hosting a bounded number of live apps, plus credits (at the existing published rate) for generation. That also keeps the credit unit honest: it still means model spend and only model spend.

Second consequence: SIGNUP_GRANT is 750 credits and one measured marketing build was 472. A Pro app build will land in the same range or higher. The free grant cannot fund a Pro build and Pro must not be reachable from the free tier at all — otherwise scripted signups mint app backends.

RECOMMENDATION: subscription + credits. Exact numbers in the pricing card.

########## [23] Build the App Kernel — one shared foundation, not eight
The most important design call in this plan: do NOT build eight independent app foundations. Build ONE kernel and make each vertical a thin configuration on top of it. Eight foundations is eight things to keep secure, eight things to keep compiling, and eight places for the same authorization bug.

The kernel ships pre-built and the model never writes any of it:
  - auth screens (login, signup, forgot password, invite acceptance) wired to app-user auth
  - the data SDK and typed hooks generated from src/schema.ts
  - an app shell: nav, responsive layout, user menu, role-aware routing
  - the CRUD engine: list with filter/sort/paginate, detail view, create/edit form generated from the schema, delete with confirmation
  - form controls with validation wired to the same schema, so validation is declared once
  - empty states, loading skeletons, error boundaries, toasts, an offline banner
  - a settings page and a light/dark theme system

What the model writes for any given app: src/schema.ts (entities and fields), a theme/branding file, copy, and two to four vertical-specific screens the CRUD engine cannot express — a pipeline board, a calendar, an invoice preview.

That ratio is the entire product thesis. It is also what makes the verticals cheap to add: once the kernel exists, a new foundation is a schema plus a screen or two, which is days rather than weeks.

########## [32] Ship local-only apps first — the cheap step that needs no backend
Before any of the infrastructure above exists, there is a shippable increment that requires no data service, no auth, no CSP change and no new dependency tree: apps that persist to IndexedDB in the visitor's own browser.

That is genuinely useful for a real class of app — a personal habit or workout tracker, a budget sheet, a checklist, a study planner, a single-person stock count — and all of it works under `connect-src 'none'` today, unchanged.

It is worth doing for three reasons beyond the feature itself: it proves the kernel's CRUD engine, form generation and schema-driven UI against real usage before any of it is load-bearing for customer data; it gives the Pro tier something to sell on day one; and it tells us whether people actually want apps or just say they do.

The non-negotiable part is labelling. The UI must say, in the editor and on the published app, that data lives only in this browser and clearing site data destroys it. That is the same standard lib/templates.ts already holds itself to when it says a restaurant template has no reservation system. Selling a local-only 'CRM' without that sentence would be exactly the 'pretends to work' failure the system prompt in lib/agent.ts forbids.

########## [6] Replace the whole-tree file dump with a manifest plus a read_file tool
describeFiles() in lib/agent.ts concatenates every file's full contents into the request message. With nine small foundation files that is fine — roughly 1,400 tokens. With a 40-60 file app kernel it is ~27,000 tokens of context the model must carry on every turn, most of which it will never need to look at, and which crowds out the reasoning budget for the part that matters.

Change: send a compact manifest instead — path, one-line purpose, byte size, and for kernel files an exported-symbol list — and add a `read_file` tool alongside write_file/delete_file so the agent pulls in only what it is about to edit. Route it through the same normalizePath() guard, and cap total bytes read per build so a confused agent cannot page in the whole kernel one file at a time and reinvent the problem.

This is what makes 'the foundation carries most of the app' actually reduce cost rather than increase it. A foundation that ships 50 files but is invisible in context is a pure win; a foundation that ships 50 files and inlines all of them every turn is a tax the customer pays on code they did not ask the model to write.

Note the SDK engine (lib/agent-sdk.ts) already has this shape — it reads files from disk on demand. This brings the API engine, which is what we actually bill on, to parity.

########## [24] Foundation 1: Internal admin / ops console — build this one first
Build this before any named vertical. It is the kernel with almost nothing on top, so it proves the kernel end to end while adding the least new surface, and it is genuinely the most useful foundation: most 'I need a CRM' requests are really 'I need a private table with a form and permissions'.

Ships pre-built: everything in the kernel, plus a generic entity console — any collection declared in the schema automatically gets list, filter, detail, create, edit, delete, a CSV export, a per-record change log, and role-based visibility.
Model generates: src/schema.ts, branding, nav labels, and any custom column formatting. Realistically 3-5 files.
Data model: user-declared collections, plus AuditEntry (actor, action, collection, record_id, before, after, at).

Credit estimate — LABELLED A GUESS, arithmetic shown. Anchor: the measured marketing build wrote 13 files / 22,568 output tokens / 472 credits, of which 169 credits were output and 303 were context. Here the model writes ~4 files, call it 6,000-9,000 output tokens => 6,000 x $15/MTok = $0.09 to 9,000 x $15 = $0.135, i.e. 45-68 credits of output. Context depends entirely on the two cost cards above: with the manifest and cache breakpoints in place, call it 80-150 credits. Total ~130-220 credits.
From scratch: not merely expensive but probably impossible on the current loop (see the MAX_TURNS card); if it completed it would be roughly 2,000-3,000 credits. Saving therefore ~10x, but the number that should be quoted internally is the absolute one — ~150-250 credits, which is CHEAPER than today's marketing site build.

########## [25] Foundation 2: CRM
The headline foundation and the one the tier is being asked for. Build it second, once the console has proved the kernel.

Ships pre-built: contact and company records with a merge-duplicates flow; a deal pipeline as a drag-and-drop board with stage transitions; an activity timeline (notes, calls, emails logged manually); tasks with due dates and an overdue view; saved filters; CSV import with column mapping — import is the feature that decides whether a real business ever adopts it, and it is far too fiddly and too easy to get subtly wrong to leave to generation.
Model generates: the pipeline stage list and their labels, custom fields per entity, branding, and the dashboard tiles that matter for that business.
Data model: Contact, Company, Deal (stage, value, close date, owner), Activity (polymorphic on contact/company/deal), Task, plus per-record owner_id for scoping.

Credit estimate — GUESS, arithmetic shown. Model writes schema + stages + ~4 custom screens/tiles, call it 10-16 files and 14,000-22,000 output tokens => $0.21-$0.33 output = 105-165 credits, plus 100-200 credits of context = roughly 200-370 credits total. Compare with the from-scratch figure in the thesis card (~2,500 credits, and likely a non-completion). Saving ~7-12x.

Note the honest headline: 370 credits is LESS than the 472-credit marketing site we actually measured. A CRM built on a kernel costs about what a landing page costs today — which is a far better sentence than 'apps are cheaper than they would be'.

########## [27] Foundation 4: Booking and scheduling
Ships pre-built, because every one of these is a place a generated implementation would be quietly wrong: the availability engine (business hours, per-staff schedules, buffers, lead time, blackout dates, timezone handling); slot generation and the double-booking guard, which must be a server-side constraint in the data service and not a client-side check; the public booking flow; cancel and reschedule with tokenised links; the admin day/week view; and confirmation and reminder emails.
Model generates: the service list with durations and prices, business hours, staff names, cancellation policy copy, branding, and the public page design.
Data model: Service, StaffMember, AvailabilityRule, Blackout, Appointment (with a uniqueness constraint on staff + time range), Customer.

Two things to be explicit about. Timezones: a booking app that gets DST wrong sends a real customer to a closed door, which is the exact harm the current system prompt's 'never invent opening hours' rule exists to prevent — so timezone handling belongs in the kernel, tested, not in generated code. Payments: taking a deposit means card handling; recommend v1 links out to an existing payment link rather than processing anything, consistent with how lib/templates.ts already handles bookings today.

Credit estimate — GUESS: model writes ~8-12 files, 12,000-18,000 output tokens => 90-135 credits output, ~100-180 context, total ~190-320 credits. The availability engine is the expensive part and the model never writes it.

########## [28] Foundation 5: Inventory tracker
The most self-contained foundation and a good candidate to build in parallel with the CRM, since it needs little beyond the kernel.

Ships pre-built: items with SKU and attributes; multiple locations; a stock-movement ledger with stock-on-hand DERIVED from movements rather than stored as a mutable counter (a mutable quantity column is the classic inventory bug — two concurrent adjustments and the count is wrong forever, and it is the same read-then-write shape audit finding M1 identifies in Kodely's own credit ledger); low-stock thresholds with alerts; suppliers and purchase orders; CSV import/export; and a barcode-friendly search.
Model generates: categories, custom attributes per item type, reorder thresholds, branding, and the dashboard.
Data model: Item, Location, StockMovement (item, location, delta, reason, actor, at), Supplier, PurchaseOrder.

Credit estimate — GUESS: ~6-10 files, 9,000-14,000 output tokens => 68-105 credits output, ~80-150 context, total ~150-260 credits.

########## [33] Write a separate system prompt for app generation
Do not extend the SYSTEM prompt in lib/agent.ts. Fork it. The current prompt is tightly written against the marketing-site contract and several of its hardest rules become actively wrong for Pro:

  - 'NO external requests ... no fetch/XHR to other origins' — a Pro app's entire purpose is calling the data service.
  - 'There is no backend, so anything needing a server cannot function. Do not build a contact form, booking form, newsletter signup, login, cart or checkout that appears functional' — this forbids literally every Pro foundation.
  - 'this is a single-page app ... not separate .html files' — the kernel has routing.

Leaving both products on one prompt means every future edit risks breaking the other, on the one file where a regression is most expensive and least visible.

The app prompt needs its own hard constraints, which are different but no less strict: never write a permission check (declare it in src/schema.ts); never call fetch directly (use the SDK); never touch kernel files; never write money or date arithmetic that the kernel already provides. Keep the two rules that transfer unchanged and matter more here than they did before — never invent facts about a real business, and never build something that only pretends to work.

Also extend PROTECTED_PATHS/PROTECTED_PATTERNS in lib/agent.ts so kernel files are unwritable. The prompt saying 'don't touch the kernel' is a request; the path guard is a rule, and audit finding C2 is the standing evidence for why that distinction matters.

# Pro foundations

A **foundation** is a pre-built app that a generation edits rather than writes.
`lib/foundation.ts` (singular) is the marketing-site starter every project uses
today: nine small files, a blank page and four UI primitives.
`lib/foundations/` (plural) is the Pro equivalent — whole applications, shipped
working, where the model supplies a schema and a dashboard instead of an app.

There is one so far: **`client-tracker`**. This document says what it is, what
it cannot do, and — the part worth reading — whether the "a foundation makes
generation cheaper" claim actually survives contact with the billing model.

---

## 1. What is built

**A single-user CRM that runs entirely in the visitor's own browser.** No
server, no account, no network request of any kind. Data lives in
`localStorage` on one device.

That shape is not a compromise chosen for speed; it is the only app shape the
current architecture permits. Generated sites are static files served under
`connect-src 'none'` (the CSP in `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts`),
with `react` and `react-dom` as the only runtime dependencies and no
`npm install` per generation (`lib/build-site.ts` symlinks one pre-installed
tree). There is no backend a generated app could talk to. Everything else on
the board's Pro column is blocked behind the backend decision; this is not.

### The split: kernel vs app

25 files, 105KB. The point is the ratio between the two halves.

| | files | bytes | est. tokens |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Kernel** — pre-built, model never touches it | 19 | 90,146 | ~25,000 |
| **App** — schema, branding, dashboard, `<head>` | 6 | 15,551 | ~4,300 |

The kernel is `src/kernel/**`: the `localStorage` store with cross-tab sync and
corruption handling, `useSyncExternalStore` bindings, a hash router, the whole
UI kit, schema-driven validation, formula-injection-safe CSV export, and the
CRUD engine — list with search / filter / sort, detail with related records,
create and edit forms generated from field declarations, delete with
confirmation, backup / restore / wipe, light and dark themes.

The app is `src/app/schema.ts` (collections and fields), `src/app/branding.ts`,
`src/app/Dashboard.tsx`, `src/App.tsx`, `src/index.css` and `index.html`. Adding
a field to the schema gives you a form control, a table column, a validation
rule, a detail row, a search target and a CSV column with no other edit. Adding
a collection gives you a nav item and full CRUD.

### Quality bar

The same one `lib/agent.ts` demands of generated sites: responsive down to
380px (verified — the table becomes a card stack at 640px, `body.scrollWidth`
is 380 at a 380px viewport), a real dark mode on a class the user controls
rather than a media query they cannot, `focus-visible` outlines on every
interactive element, labelled controls with `aria-invalid` and
`aria-describedby`, `aria-current` on nav, a dialog that traps Escape and
returns focus to its opener, and no external request of any kind — no fonts, no
images, no CDN. Icons are inline SVG.

---

## 2. What it honestly cannot do

This is on the record in three places: `CLIENT_TRACKER.cannot` in
`lib/foundations/client-tracker/index.ts`, a non-dismissible footer on every
screen of the app, and a four-bullet explanation on the app's own Data page.

- **It cannot be shared.** One browser, one device. A second person or a second
  device opens an empty app. There is no "our team's CRM" version of this.
- **It cannot back itself up.** Clearing site data, a privacy cleaner or a
  browser reset destroys everything with no warning and no recovery. The JSON
  export is the only copy that survives, which is why the export is one click
  from every screen and the delete flow makes you type `DELETE`.
- **It cannot send or receive anything.** No email, no SMS, no calendar sync,
  no payment, no import from another system except pasted JSON.
- **It has no accounts and no permissions.** Whoever can open the browser
  profile can read everything.
- **It must not hold data anyone is legally required to protect.** Nothing is
  encrypted at rest and nothing is audited.

The kernel enforces the first two in the UI rather than leaving them to the
generated copy. `StorageFooter` in `src/kernel/AppShell.tsx` is not dismissible
and does not take a prop that could turn it off. That is deliberate: the
failure it guards against — a year of client history lost to a cache clear —
happens exactly once per user and cannot be undone. Selling a local-only "CRM"
without that sentence would be the "pretends to work" failure the system prompt
in `lib/agent.ts` already forbids.

---

## 3. Proof it compiles

Built through the real `buildSite` from `lib/build-site.ts` — the same function
production and the eval harness call, not a copy.

Without it the path falls back to `/home/kodely/kodely-foundation` and every

The output was then served under the production CSP verbatim and clicked
through in a browser: create with validation rejecting a bad email, save,
persist to `localStorage`, detail view, a related-record link that pre-fills the
parent, the dashboard tiles, currency and relative-date formatting, the list

## 4. The credit arithmetic — does the thesis hold?

The claim under test: *pre-built foundations make generation cheaper, because
the model writes less.* It is a real claim with a real counter-argument —
`describeFiles()` in `lib/agent.ts` inlines every byte of every project file
into the request **on every turn**, so a big foundation is a recurring context
charge, not a one-off saving.

### The rate card

From `lib/models.ts`, `claude-sonnet-5`, in micro-dollars per token. One credit
is 2,000 micros (`MICROS_PER_CREDIT`, `lib/credits.ts`).

| | µ$/token |
| --- | ---: |
| output | 15.00 |
| input (uncached) | 3.00 |
| cache write | 3.75 |
| cache read | 0.30 |

### The measured anchor

One real marketing build, `scripts/eval/results/2026-08-21T17-44-48-482Z-verify.json`
— 13 files written, compiled first try, 472 credits:

| | tokens | µ$ | share |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| output | 22,568 | 338,520 | 36% |
| cache read | 1,076,680 | 323,004 | 34% |
| cache write | 74,345 | 278,794 | 30% |
| input | 992 | 2,976 | 0.3% |
| **total** | | **943,294** | = **472 credits** |

**Two facts fall straight out of this table, and both are load-bearing.**

First, **output is only 36% of a build's cost.** Nearly two thirds is context.
So "the model writes less" is an argument about the smaller half of the bill.

Second, **the request prefix is being served from cache.** `input_tokens` is
992 for the entire build — everything else was a cache read. The final prefix is
about 77,000 tokens (74,345 cache-written plus system and tools), and 1,076,680
cache-read tokens against it means **the average context token was billed as a
cache read roughly 14 times.**

### The per-token comparison

A token of foundation, placed in the request prefix, costs one cache write plus
one cache read per subsequent call. A token the model writes instead costs
output price, and then *also* joins the prefix and is re-read.

```
in cached prefix:   3.75 + 0.30 x (reads)
written as output: 15.00 + 0.30 x (reads after it was written)
```

| re-reads | prefix token | output token | ratio |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2 (turns=3) | 4.35 µ$ | 15.30 µ$ | 3.5x |
| 4 (turns=5) | 4.95 µ$ | 15.90 µ$ | 3.2x |
| 7 (turns=8, `MAX_TURNS`) | 5.85 µ$ | 16.80 µ$ | 2.9x |
| 13 (the 14x measured above) | 7.65 µ$ | 18.60 µ$ | 2.4x |

**Break-even is 38.5 re-reads.** `MAX_TURNS` is 8, so within one build the
foundation physically cannot reach the point where carrying it costs more than
generating it.

### What that means for this foundation, in credits

The Pro foundation as `describeFiles()` would send it is 108,797 characters ≈
**30,221 tokens** (estimated at 3.6 chars/token; calibrated against the board's
own "nine small foundation files ≈ 1,400 tokens" figure for the marketing
starter, and the estimate only scales the comparison, it does not change which
side wins).

| | credits per build |
| --- | ---: |
| Foundation inlined by `describeFiles()`, 8 turns, cached | **88** |
| Same, but the cache misses entirely (uncached input x 8) | **363** |
| Same, cold cache write only (a single-turn build) | **57** |
| Model writes those 25,000 kernel tokens itself instead | **254** (before thinking tokens) |
| Manifest instead of the dump (1,213 tokens) | **3.5** |
| *For scale: today's marketing foundation dump* | *8.4* |

### Verdict

**The thesis holds — by about 3x, not 10x, and only because of prefix caching.**

- Shipping the kernel as context costs ~88 credits a build. Having the model
  write the same code costs ~254 credits of output *before* thinking tokens,
  before the repair turns that a 25-file app would provoke, and before the very
  real possibility that it never completes inside `MAX_TURNS` at all. So the
  foundation wins on cost and wins much harder on whether the build finishes.
- **But 88 credits is a tax on every build, including edits that never touch
  the kernel.** "Make the header blue" pays the full 88 credits to re-send a
  CSV exporter and a date formatter the model will not read. Against a measured
  ~172-credit edit, that is a **~50% surcharge on every follow-up turn**. This
  is the honest bad news, and it is the strongest possible argument for the
  board's manifest card.
- **The saving is entirely contingent on the prefix being cached.** At
  30,221 tokens, an uncached foundation costs 363 credits a build — *more
  expensive than having the model write it.* Today `lib/agent.ts` sets
  `cache_control` only on the system prompt; the messages array carries no
  breakpoint, and the caching visible in the measured build is therefore not
  something the code explicitly asks for. **Before a foundation this size ships,
  the cache breakpoints on the messages array are not an optimisation — they
  are the difference between the foundation saving 166 credits a build and
  costing 109 more.**
- **The manifest changes the answer from "3x better" to "25x better."** Sending
  the manifest (`describeManifest()` in `lib/foundations/types.ts`: path,
  purpose, byte size and exported symbols per file) is 1,213 tokens against
  30,221 — **4%** — for 3.5 credits a build instead of 88. Every foundation file
  already carries the `purpose` and `exports` strings this needs. A foundation
  that ships 25 files and is invisible in context is a pure win; one that ships
  25 files and inlines them every turn is a tax the customer pays on code they
  did not ask for.

**The number to quote internally:** with the manifest and cache breakpoints in
place, a client-tracker build should be roughly *4 credits of foundation
context + ~36 credits of output for the six app files + the ordinary context
growth of the conversation* — comfortably under the 472 credits a marketing
site measured. An app costing less than a landing page is a better sentence
than "apps are cheaper than they would have been", and this arithmetic supports
it — but only after two changes that are not in this directory.

---

## 5. Wiring it in — changes needed outside `lib/foundations/**`

Nothing imports `lib/foundations/` yet. It compiles, it builds and it runs, but
no generation can reach it. In rough order of necessity:

1. **`lib/agent.ts` — a separate system prompt for app generation.** Do not
   extend `SYSTEM`. Several of its hardest rules are actively wrong here: "this
   is a single-page app ... not separate .html files" (the kernel routes), and
   "Do not build a contact form, booking form, newsletter signup, login, cart
   or checkout that appears functional" (a CRUD app is nothing but forms). Two
   rules must transfer unchanged and matter more here: never invent facts about
   a real business, and never build something that only pretends to work.
2. **`lib/agent.ts` — `PROTECTED_PATHS` must cover `src/kernel/`.** The prompt
   saying "do not touch the kernel" is a request; `isProtectedPath` is a rule.
   A one-line pattern `/^src\/kernel\//` does it. `kernelPaths()` in
   `lib/foundations/types.ts` returns the exact list.
3. **`lib/agent.ts` — cache breakpoints on the messages array, and a `read_file`
   tool plus manifest instead of `describeFiles()`.** Per section 4, the first
   is a correctness requirement for the cost model and the second is where the
   whole saving lives.
4. **`lib/build-site.ts` and `prisma/schema.prisma` — a `foundation` parameter
   and a column recording which foundation a project was created from.** Not
   needed for `client-tracker`, which adds no dependency and compiles against
   the existing tree unchanged; needed the moment a foundation wants one.
5. **Project creation (`lib/seed-project.ts`, `app/api/projects/route.ts`)** —
   seed from `foundationFiles(getFoundation(id))` instead of `FOUNDATION_FILES`,
   and surface `foundation.cannot` in the picker before the user chooses, not
   after.
6. **`app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts` — nothing.** That is the point.
   The CSP does not move for a client-only app, which is the entire reason this
   one could be built now.

---

## 6. The next three or four

In the order they should be built, each still client-only, each reusing the
same kernel with a different `src/app/**`:

1. **Booking log** (~1 week). Services, staff, appointments, a day and week
   view. The kernel needs a `time` field kind and a calendar screen; the
   availability engine and double-booking guard are *not* buildable here —
   without a server there is nothing to enforce a uniqueness constraint
   against, so this is an appointment **log** for one person's own diary, and
   it must be named and described as one. Timezone handling belongs in
   `src/kernel/format.ts` where it is tested, never in generated code.
2. **Stock count** (~3 days). Items, locations, and a movement ledger with
   stock-on-hand *derived from movements* rather than stored as a mutable
   counter. The kernel needs one new thing — a derived/computed field — and
   gets the cheapest possible proof of it. A mutable quantity column is the
   classic inventory bug and the same read-then-write shape audit finding M1
   identifies in Kodely's own credit ledger.
3. **Quote and invoice builder** (~1 week). Line items, totals, a printable
   view. Needs a repeating-group field kind (the kernel's biggest genuine gap)
   and money arithmetic in integer minor units in the kernel — never in
   generated code, and never in floats. Print CSS instead of PDF generation,
   because a PDF library is a dependency and there is no install step.
4. **Personal admin console** (~2 days). The kernel with almost nothing on top:
   any declared collection gets full CRUD and a CSV export. Cheapest of the
   four and the best regression test of the kernel, since it is the kernel with
   the vertical removed. Worth building *last* here rather than first as the
   board suggests, because after three real verticals it becomes a genuine
   check that nothing vertical-specific leaked into `src/kernel/`.

**What none of them can be.** Every one of these is single-user and
single-device, and each one wants to be shared more than the last — a booking
log that a customer cannot book into is half a product, and an invoice nobody
can be sent is less than that. That ceiling is not a gap in the kernel; it is
`connect-src 'none'` plus "no server", and no amount of client-side code moves
it.

### What would have to change for a genuinely multi-user app

Three things, in strict order, and the first two are decisions rather than work:

1. **Move published site serving off the app origin.** Sites render today at
   `kodely.me/api/site/...`, first-party to the app. `connect-src 'none'` is
   the single control stopping hostile generated script from calling `/api/*`
   with the victim's cookies, and `docs/security/audit-2026-08.md` cites it as
   the reason finding H1 is High rather than Critical. Opening `connect-src`
   before that move makes the current position materially worse.
2. **Decide whether Kodely will be a processor of its customers' end-user
   data.** The moment a plumber's client list lives on Kodely's servers, that
   is a DPA, a sub-processor list, breach-notification duties, and deletion
   requests about people Kodely has no relationship with. This is the actual
   product being sold and it is not an engineering call.
3. **Then, and only then, one first-party data service** at a single origin,
   reached by exactly one new `connect-src` entry (`https://data.kodely.app`,
   deliberately not `'self'`), with declarative per-project schemas, first-party
   end-user auth, and **server-enforced** row scoping. The model would declare a
   schema — the same `src/app/schema.ts` this foundation already uses — and
   write UI, never a permission check and never a query. The kernel's data layer
   would swap `src/kernel/store.ts` for an SDK behind the same
   `useCollection` / `useStore` interface, which is why that interface is worth
   keeping narrow now.

Until then, "single-user, on this device, and it says so" is not a lesser
product. It is the honest one.

Done. Everything is in `lib/foundations/**` and `docs/pro-foundations.md`; no file outside that scope was touched.

## What I built and why

**`lib/foundations/client-tracker` — a single-user CRM that runs entirely in the browser.** I picked the CRM over the booking log because it's the headline foundation on the board (card 25) *and* because booking is the one vertical that is quietly broken without a server: the double-booking guard has to be a server-side constraint, so a client-only "booking system" would be exactly the pretends-to-work failure `lib/agent.ts` forbids. A client tracker is genuinely complete for one person.

Structured as **kernel + vertical**, per board card 23: 25 files, 105KB.

- **Kernel (19 files, 90KB, model never writes it):** localStorage store with cross-tab sync, corruption handling and quota detection; `useSyncExternalStore` bindings; hash router; whole UI kit; schema-driven validation; formula-injection-safe CSV; and the CRUD engine — list with search/filter/sort, detail with related records, forms generated from field declarations, delete confirmation, backup/restore/wipe, light+dark theme.
- **App (6 files, 15KB, what a generation writes):** `src/app/schema.ts`, branding, dashboard, `App.tsx`, `index.css`, `index.html`.

Honesty is enforced in code, not copy: `StorageFooter` is on every screen, takes no prop that could disable it, and the Data page spells out the four consequences in plain words. `CLIENT_TRACKER.cannot` carries the same five limits as data.

## Proof it compiles

Through the real `buildSite`, with `.env` loaded (`KODELY_FOUNDATION_DIR=C:\Users\edmem\kodely-foundation`): **28 source files → BUILD OK in 1563 ms**, dist 240KB JS + 29KB CSS + index.html. Then served under the production CSP verbatim and clicked through in a browser: create with validation rejecting a bad email, persist, detail view, related-record prefill, dashboard tiles, currency/relative dates, list table, Data page. Zero console messages, zero CSP violations, no horizontal overflow at 380px.

Gate: `tsc` 0 errors, `eslint app lib components` 0 errors 0 warnings, **303/303 tests pass** (the suite grew from 209 during the session — another agent is working in this tree, and `lib/foundation.ts` changed under me mid-run; I did not touch it).

## The credit arithmetic — verdict

Anchor is the real measured build in `scripts/eval/results/2026-08-21T...verify.json`: 13 files, 472 credits. Two facts fall out of it:

1. **Output is only 36% of cost.** Cache read 34%, cache write 30%, uncached input 0.3%.
2. **The prefix is being cached** (`input_tokens` = 992 for the whole build), and cache reads / final prefix ≈ **14x amplification**.

Per-token, sonnet-5 rates: a prefix token costs `3.75 + 0.30 × reads`; an output token costs `15.00 + 0.30 × later reads`. **Break-even is 38.5 re-reads; `MAX_TURNS` is 8.**

Foundation = 108,797 chars ≈ **30,221 tokens**:

| | credits/build |
|---|---:|
| Inlined by `describeFiles()`, 8 turns, cached | **88** |
| Same, uncached | **363** |
| Model writes the 25k kernel tokens itself | **254** (pre-thinking) |
| Manifest instead (1,213 tokens) | **3.5** |

**The thesis holds, by ~3x, not 10x — and with two caveats that matter more than the headline:**

- **88 credits is a tax on every build, including edits.** Against a measured ~172-credit edit, that's a **~50% surcharge on every follow-up turn** for re-sending a CSV exporter the model won't read.
- **The saving is entirely contingent on prefix caching.** Uncached, the foundation costs 363 credits — *more than having the model write it*. `lib/agent.ts` sets `cache_control` only on the system prompt; the messages array has no breakpoint. Board card 5 is not an optimisation, it's the difference between saving 166 credits and losing 109.
- **The manifest is where the win actually is:** 1,213 vs 30,221 tokens = 4%, i.e. 3.5 credits instead of 88. Every foundation file already carries the `purpose`/`exports` strings; `describeManifest()` is implemented and tested by eye.

## Changes needed elsewhere (described, not made)

Nothing imports `lib/foundations/` yet. In order: (1) fork the system prompt in `lib/agent.ts` — its "no functional forms" and "single-page, not separate .html" rules are actively wrong for an app; (2) add `/^src\/kernel\//` to `PROTECTED_PATTERNS` (`kernelPaths()` returns the exact list); (3) cache breakpoints on the messages array + `read_file` tool replacing the whole-tree dump; (4) `foundation` param on `buildSite` + a Project column — *not* needed for this one, which adds no dependency; (5) seed from `foundationFiles(getFoundation(id))` and show `foundation.cannot` in the picker *before* the choice. The CSP needs no change at all — that's the point.

## What it cannot do, and what multi-user would take

It cannot be shared, back itself up, send anything, or have accounts. Next foundations, all still client-only: booking **log** (not a booking system), stock count with derived-from-ledger quantities, quote/invoice builder, personal admin console. Each wants to be shared more than the last.

Genuinely multi-user needs three things in strict order: move published site serving off the app origin (`connect-src 'none'` is why audit finding H1 is High not Critical); decide whether Kodely becomes a processor of customers' end-user data (a business decision, not an engineering one); then one first-party data service at a single origin with exactly one new `connect-src` entry and server-enforced row scoping. The kernel is shaped for that swap — `src/kernel/store.ts` sits behind a deliberately narrow `useStore`/`useCollection` interface an SDK could replace without touching a screen.
